howItWorks.intro: This estimator translates everyday eating patterns — how often you eat out, what you cook with at home, how much packaged and fried food you eat — into an approximate gram count of seed oil and linoleic acid. It is not a food diary or a lab test; it is a rough gauge built from typical serving sizes and typical oil use in restaurant kitchens and food manufacturing, so treat the output as an order-of-magnitude estimate rather than a precise figure.
rules: Restaurant meals: most restaurants cook with soybean or canola oil — estimated 2-4 tbsp seed oil per meal
Cooking oil: home cooking with seed oils adds ~1-2 tbsp per meal; olive oil, butter, and coconut oil contain minimal linoleic acid
Packaged foods: most contain soybean, canola, or sunflower oil — ~0.5-1 tbsp seed oil per serving
Fried/snack foods: chips, fries, and fried foods are major sources — 1-3 tbsp per serving
Dressings and sauces: most commercial dressings are soybean oil-based — ~0.5-1 tbsp per serving
Linoleic acid: the primary omega-6 fatty acid in seed oils, making up 50-60% of soybean and corn oil
howItWorks.outro: For context: a single restaurant stir-fry or a fast-food-sized portion of fries can each supply 10-16g of linoleic acid — more than a home-cooked, olive-oil-based dinner would typically contain. Someone eating out for most lunches and dinners, snacking on chips a few times a week, and using bottled dressing daily can land well past 50g of seed oil equivalent in a single day, largely without noticing, since none of these foods are labeled "seed oil" on the package. Whether a high omega-6 intake from these oils carries meaningful health risk is genuinely unsettled in nutrition research — some researchers point to oxidation products and skewed omega-6:omega-3 ratios as a concern, while others point to large trials and meta-analyses showing neutral or favorable effects of linoleic acid on cardiovascular risk markers. This calculator estimates intake; it does not settle that debate, and nothing here is medical advice.

faq.question: What actually counts as a seed oil?
faq.answer: Seed oils are oils extracted from the seeds of plants rather than from fruits, nuts, or animal fat — soybean oil, canola (rapeseed) oil, corn oil, sunflower oil, safflower oil, cottonseed oil, and grapeseed oil are the most common in the U.S. food supply. Soybean oil alone accounts for the majority of added fat in U.S. packaged and restaurant food because it's cheap to produce at scale.

faq.question: Why does this calculator ask about restaurant meals separately from home cooking?
faq.answer: Because the two behave very differently. A home cook who buys olive oil can largely control their own intake, but restaurant kitchens choose oil based on cost and shelf life, and soybean or canola oil dominates commercial fryers and saute pans. Someone who eats out four nights a week can end up with a higher seed oil estimate than someone who cooks with canola oil at home every single night.

faq.question: Is a high omega-6:omega-3 ratio actually harmful?
faq.answer: It depends who you ask. Some nutrition researchers argue that a skewed ratio — commonly estimated at 10:1 to 20:1 in modern Western diets versus roughly 1:1 to 4:1 before industrial oil refining — promotes a more pro-inflammatory state. Other researchers, including authors of several meta-analyses on linoleic acid and cardiovascular disease, find no consistent evidence that linoleic acid itself raises inflammatory markers or cardiovascular risk at typical intakes. This remains an active research question rather than a settled one, and this calculator doesn't take a side in it — it estimates intake only.

faq.question: How accurate is the gram estimate?
faq.answer: It's a rough approximation, not a lab measurement. The calculator applies typical serving-size assumptions — for example, 2-4 tablespoons of oil per restaurant meal — drawn from general food-service patterns, but actual oil use varies by restaurant, brand, and recipe. Treat the output as a directional estimate for comparing scenarios, not a precise figure for clinical use.

faq.question: Which oils have the least linoleic acid?
faq.answer: Coconut oil and butter are among the lowest, typically under 2g of linoleic acid per tablespoon. Olive oil, avocado oil, tallow, and lard are also comparatively low, generally in the 1-2g range per tablespoon, compared to roughly 7-8g per tablespoon in soybean or corn oil.

faq.question: What's a practical first step to lower my number?
faq.answer: Based on how the calculator weights inputs, cutting restaurant and takeout meals has the biggest single effect for most people, followed by swapping bottled dressing for a homemade vinaigrette and changing your everyday cooking oil. Packaged snack foods matter too, but typically contribute less than the other three categories unless eaten several times a day. As always, this is general information, not personalized medical or dietary advice.

howWeCalculate.intro: Each answer you select carries an assigned oil-and-linoleic-acid weight drawn from typical serving sizes: a restaurant meal is assumed to use 2-4 tablespoons of frying or saute oil, a packaged snack roughly 0.5-1 tablespoon, and a home-cooked meal made with seed oil around 1-2 tablespoons. The calculator sums the weighted contribution from all five inputs, converts tablespoons of oil to grams at about 13.5g per tablespoon, then applies the linoleic acid share typical of soybean, corn, and sunflower oil to produce the linoleic acid figure. Calories are derived at roughly 120 per tablespoon of oil, and the annual total simply multiplies the daily estimate by 365.
steps: Estimate how many meals you eat out or order in per week, then pick the oil you reach for most often when cooking at home.
Add your typical packaged-food, fried/snack-food, and dressing-or-sauce frequency — these three categories drive most of the hidden seed oil in a typical Western diet.
Click Estimate Seed Oil Intake to convert your selections into daily and annual totals, calories from oil, and an omega-6:omega-3 ratio estimate.
Compare your result against the roughly 40-80g/day range typical of U.S. diets, then check the food-by-food chart below to see which specific items are driving your number.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These figures come from typical serving-size and oil-content assumptions, not from a food log or lab analysis of your actual meals — treat them as a directional estimate. If you're changing your diet for a diagnosed condition, talk to a doctor or registered dietitian rather than relying on this calculator alone.

whenToUse.intro: Use this calculator when you want a rough read on how much of your daily fat intake is coming from industrially refined seed oils rather than olive oil, butter, or other traditional fats — whether you're simply curious, experimenting with an omega-6 reduction, or trying to see where your restaurant and snacking habits actually land you.
scenarios: You've started reading ingredient labels and want to know whether your current eating pattern is genuinely high in seed oil or just feels that way.
You're deciding whether switching your home cooking oil from canola to olive or avocado oil would meaningfully change your total intake, or whether restaurant meals dominate the number regardless.
You eat out often and want a ballpark figure for how many tablespoons of soybean or canola oil that adds up to over a week or a year.
You're trying to shift your omega-6 to omega-3 ratio and want a starting estimate before tracking more precisely with a food diary.
You want to see, before changing anything, which single habit — restaurant meals, packaged snacks, or bottled dressings — contributes the most to your estimate.

sections.title: What Counts as a Seed Oil?
sections.body: Seed oils — soybean, canola (rapeseed), corn, sunflower, safflower, cottonseed, and grapeseed oil — became the default cooking fat in American restaurants and food manufacturing over the last century because they're cheap to produce, neutral in flavor, and shelf-stable. That makes them easy to eat in large amounts without realizing it: a stir-fry, a bag of chips, and a bottle of ranch dressing can all be soybean-oil-based even though none of them say "seed oil" on the front label. Oils like olive, avocado, and coconut oil, along with butter, ghee, and tallow, are not seed oils and generally carry far less linoleic acid. This calculator takes five everyday inputs — how often you eat out, what oil you cook with at home, how many packaged and fried foods you eat, and how often you use bottled dressing or mayo — and converts them into an estimated daily gram count of seed oil and linoleic acid, an annual total, and a rough omega-6-to-omega-3 ratio.

sections.title: Why Track Linoleic Acid Specifically?
sections.body: Linoleic acid is the omega-6 fatty acid that makes up roughly half of soybean and corn oil by weight, and it's the fatty acid most often cited in the seed oil debate. Some researchers argue that rising linoleic acid intake over the last century has shifted the body's omega-6-to-omega-3 balance in a way that may promote low-grade inflammation. Others point to randomized trials and large meta-analyses finding linoleic acid neutral or even favorable for LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular outcomes. Both camps largely agree on how much linoleic acid is actually in these oils — they disagree on what that intake means for long-term health. This calculator stays on the measurement side of that argument: it estimates intake, not risk, and it isn't a substitute for medical advice.

sections.title: A Worked Example: One Day of Meals
sections.body: Take a fairly ordinary day. Two slices of toast at breakfast contribute about 0.3 tbsp of seed oil (≈1.2g linoleic acid) from the bread itself. A fast-casual lunch salad topped with 2 tablespoons of bottled dressing adds roughly 1 tbsp of seed oil (≈4g). A granola bar as an afternoon snack adds another 0.5 tbsp (≈2g). A restaurant stir-fry for dinner, cooked in soybean oil, adds about 2.5 tbsp (≈10g). A small bag of chips later in the evening adds a further 2.5 tbsp (≈10g). Add it up and that's roughly 6.8 tablespoons of seed oil and about 27g of linoleic acid from just five items — before counting any oil used to cook the toast or dress a side dish. Stack a couple more restaurant meals or snack servings into the week, and it's easy to see how someone eating an ordinary American diet, without ever intentionally choosing seed oil, lands in the 40-80g-per-day range this calculator is built around.

howToSteps.title: Estimate Your Weekly Restaurant and Takeout Meals
howToSteps.description: Pick the range that best matches how often you ate food someone else cooked last week. Restaurant meals are usually the single largest source of hidden seed oil, since most commercial kitchens cook with soybean or canola oil by default.

howToSteps.title: Choose Your Primary At-Home Cooking Oil
howToSteps.description: Select the oil you reach for most when cooking at home. Olive oil, butter, ghee, coconut oil, and avocado oil all carry far less linoleic acid than canola, soybean, corn, or sunflower oil.

howToSteps.title: Add Packaged Food, Fried Snack, and Dressing Habits
howToSteps.description: Fill in how many packaged or processed servings you eat daily, how often you eat fried or snack foods, and how often you use bottled dressing, mayo, or sauce. These three habits combine with restaurant meals to make up most people's total.

howToSteps.title: Review Your Daily, Annual, and Ratio Estimates
howToSteps.description: Click Estimate Seed Oil Intake to see your daily seed oil and linoleic acid totals, the annual equivalent, calories from seed oil, and an estimated omega-6:omega-3 ratio — then check the food-by-food chart below to see which habit is driving your number.

tips: Restaurant and takeout meals usually outweigh every other input combined — if you're trying to lower your estimate, changing where you eat out or asking how food is cooked moves the number more than swapping your home cooking oil alone.

Bottled salad dressing, mayo, and sauces are an easy blind spot: two tablespoons of a typical ranch or Italian dressing carries close to 4g of linoleic acid, on par with what several slices of ordinary bread would add up to.

Olive oil, avocado oil, butter, ghee, coconut oil, tallow, and lard are not seed oils and contribute comparatively little linoleic acid — switching your home cooking oil to one of these lowers your home-cooking contribution but won't offset frequent restaurant meals or packaged snacks on its own.

If you don't know what oil a restaurant uses, soybean or canola oil is a reasonable default assumption for most U.S. chain and fast-casual kitchens — it's the industry standard because it's inexpensive and neutral-tasting.

Try running the calculator twice: once with your current habits and once with a hypothetical change, like cooking at home a few more nights a week, to see which single adjustment moves your estimate the most.
